title: Where Does Electric Charge Go? Additivity and Conservation of Charge
subject: Physics
objective: Rub a glass rod with silk and the two get charges that are always exactly equal and opposite. Rubbing moves electrons from the glass to the silk; it never makes charge. Charge is additive (the total is the algebraic sum, signs included) and conserved (the total charge of an isolated system never changes). The rule holds even when particles transform: a free neutron becomes a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, and a gamma photon near a nucleus becomes an electron and a positron, with the total charge unchanged every time.

tf.explain: It stays constant; it can be nonzero.

ar.a: Assertion: The total charge of an isolated system is always zero. Reason: Charge is conserved.
ar.r: Assertion false (it is constant, not necessarily zero); reason true.

ar.a: Assertion: Glass and silk get equal and opposite charges on rubbing. Reason: Electrons transfer from glass to silk.
ar.r: Both true; the reason explains the assertion.

short.q: Why are the charges on rubbed glass and silk equal and opposite?
short.solution: Electrons only move from glass to silk; the silk gains exactly what the glass loses, so the total stays zero.

short.q: Distinguish additivity from conservation of charge.
short.solution: Additivity: the total is the algebraic sum of the charges. Conservation: that total does not change in an isolated system.

short.q: Write neutron decay and check the charge balance.
Why can a single photon not create a pair in empty space?
short.solution: Energy and momentum cannot both be conserved; a nucleus must take the recoil momentum.
